p03-in-component.what: Boundary inside a component, one module away from the entry.

p05-siblings.what: Two boundaries as siblings, with first-screen content between them.
p05-siblings.reading: Two boundaries, one main-thread tree. They are holes in the same first frame, not two roots — nothing had to be added for the second one.

p06-nested-children.what: A boundary inside another boundary’s children.
p06-nested-children.reading: The inner boundary is inside the deferred subtree, so the main thread never reaches it: the outer fallback is the whole first frame, and `sk-b` only shows up after hydration.

p07-nested-fallback.what: A boundary inside another boundary’s fallback.
p07-nested-fallback.reading: The fold is recursive: the outer boundary is replaced by its fallback, which is itself a boundary and is replaced in turn. The first frame is the innermost fallback, `sk-inner`.

p08-in-map.what: Boundaries produced by a .map() over data.
p08-in-map.reading: The fold is syntactic and happens once, at the element in the source; how many elements the loop produces at runtime is not a question it has to answer.

p10-heavy.what: Same shape as p01, with 46 KB of business code behind the boundary.
p10-heavy.reading: The other cases are micro-apps: their main-thread chunks measure this mode's fixed overhead and little else. Here the deferred subtree is big enough to read the size column directly — the fallback still paints at 0.0, and the 46 KB is not in the main-thread chunk.

i01-aliased.what: Imported under an alias: import { Background as B }.
i01-aliased.reading: The fold follows the import binding, not the element name, so the alias is not a special case for it. The config-time scan asks the same question — does this module bind `Background` from the runtime — which is why the alias does not hide the entry from it either.

i03-reexport.what: Re-exported through a local module, then imported from there.
i03-reexport.reading: The re-export is the first shape where the two mechanisms disagree. The scan sees `boundary.js` re-export the runtime and compiles the entry, so the runtime component renders the fallback correctly — but the fold works one module at a time and cannot tell that the local `Background` binding is the runtime's, so it leaves the element alone and the deferred code stays in the chunk.

i04-wrapper.what: A user component wraps the boundary; callers never write <Background>.
i04-wrapper.reading: The boundary is real and renders correctly, but it is inside `Deferred`, while the reference to the deferred subtree lives at the *call site*, in `children`. The fold cuts the reference where the element is written; here there is no element to cut at the place that holds the reference. Correct pixels, no bundle win — and no local rewrite can recover it.

i05-dynamic-type.what: The element type is chosen at runtime.
i05-dynamic-type.reading: The element type is a value, not a name — deciding whether it is the boundary would mean evaluating the program. This is the hard limit of the static half; the runtime half still behaves, because `<Background>` is an ordinary component that renders its fallback on the main thread.

f01-static-host.what: Fallback is static host elements only.

f02-stateful-component.what: Fallback is a component using hooks.
f02-stateful-component.reading: The fallback is compiled for the main thread as ordinary code, so a component with state is not a special case — this is what rules out any design where the fallback may only be host elements.

f03-no-fallback.what: Boundary with no fallback at all.
f03-no-fallback.reading: The degenerate case: the boundary folds to nothing, so the first frame is whatever surrounds it. `hdr` paints, the boundary's own space stays empty until hydration.

f04-fallback-uses-deferred.what: The fallback renders the very component the boundary defers.
f04-fallback-uses-deferred.reading: The deferred code stays in the chunk because the author asked for it: the fallback names the same component. Correct, and the honest answer to “can I defer this?” is no — you just said you need it at 0.0.

f05-spread.what: Props spread onto the boundary — the fallback is not statically resolvable.
f05-spread.reading: Refused rather than guessed. A spread can carry `fallback`, so folding would have to pick a value the compiler cannot see; the error names the boundary and the file instead of silently producing a blank first frame.

g01-assert-folded.what: The deferred module asserts it with `import 'background-only'`.
g01-assert-folded.reading: The same shape as `p01-root`, plus an assertion in the deferred module. The fold reaches it, so the module is not in the main-thread graph and the assertion holds — and under `true` the classic build compiles it there, so the build fails. That failure is the assertion's real cost: it is not a free guardrail but a declaration that this module has no place in any main-thread-rendering build, development included, where `'auto'` always resolves to the classic path. Compare `p01-root`, which is this case without the assertion and builds in all three.

g02-assert-not-folded.what: `i04-wrapper`, with the same assertion — the case the fold cannot cut.
g02-assert-not-folded.reading: This is the deliverable of the whole matrix. `i04-wrapper` is this exact app without the assertion: it builds everywhere, paints correctly everywhere, and silently ships the deferred logic under `'auto'`/`false` — a loss nothing but reading the chunk would reveal. The assertion is on the *module*, so it does not care where the reference lives, and turns that silence into a build error naming the file.
